tagline.text: A vast Quezon City campus with the Oblation statue and the Carillon tower

location.label: Location
location.text: Diliman, Quezon City (around Osmeña Avenue and Roxas Avenue)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (Lantern Parade in December)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200–800 (per person, half a day, including food)

children.text: The Diliman campus of the national university covers about
493 hectares
. It is a green oasis in Quezon City where you can walk to the Oblation statue, the Academic Oval, the Carillon tower, the Sunken Garden and the Vargas Museum.
UP Diliman is the main campus of the University of the Philippines in Quezon City, Metro Manila. According to Wikipedia, the campus covers about
493 hectares

and had around 26,000 students in 2023. Most of the university's academic functions moved here from central Manila (Padre Faura Street) by 1949, and Diliman has been regarded as a symbol of Philippine higher education ever since. It is a living campus rather than a tourist attraction, so you enjoy architecture, sculpture, public art and shady trees amid the ordinary routines of students.
The heart of any visit is the Academic Oval, an oval ring road about
2.2 km

around. Roughly 500 acacia and fir-type trees shade it, and one lane is reserved for pedestrians and cyclists. Along the road you pass Quezon Hall (the administration building), the Oblation statue in front of it, Gonzalez Hall (home of the University Main Library) and Palma Hall, all buildings from the 1950s. Beyond the Oval, the 5-hectare Sunken Garden, the Carillon tower, the Vargas Museum and the university chapel designed by architect Leandro Locsin are spread around, so they combine well into a one-day route.

If Manila's other historic districts are about old walls and churches, Diliman is the place to see mid-20th-century Philippine modernist architecture and student culture. Wikipedia records that Gonzalez Hall was designed by architect Juan Nakpil and completed in 1950, Palma Hall was completed in 1951, and the university chapel in 1955. Add events such as the Lantern Parade in December and the UP Fair in February, and the campus feels completely different depending on when you come.

Food is another advantage. On campus there is Rodic's Diner, said to have operated since 1949, cafés at the alumni center (Bahay ng Alumni) and a food park, and the neighboring Maginhawa Street and Katipunan Avenue are known as the food-trip streets of young Quezon City. It is an easy half-day plan of walking, sightseeing and eating.

blocks.title: The Oblation statue and Quezon Hall

children.text: The Oblation, the symbol of UP, was made by sculptor Guillermo Tolentino in

. Wikipedia records that on February 12, 1949 it was moved from Padre Faura Street in Manila to the front of Quezon Hall, and that the bronze statue seen today was unveiled on November 29, 1958 and is housed at Gonzalez Hall. The lawn in front of Quezon Hall is where most visitors take their commemorative photos.
You can walk or cycle the ring road of about
2.2 km

. About 500 trees give shade, one lane is used by pedestrians and cyclists, and many residents jog here at dawn. It is fun to look for the mirrored pairs of buildings, such as Melchor Hall and Palma Hall, and Benitez Hall and Malcolm Hall.
The tower, about

(130 feet) tall, was completed in 1952 and is described as the only manually played carillon in Southeast Asia. It fell silent in 1981, was restored with new bells, and rang again at the 2007 Lantern Parade. The official UP site says the bells chime hourly and that the carillon plays Filipino songs and UP songs daily at
and

A basin-shaped lawn of about 5 hectares in the eastern part of the campus, behind Gonzalez Hall, with Malcolm Hall to the north. On ordinary days it is an open space for jogging and picnics, and every February it becomes the stage for the UP Fair, a roughly five-day music festival. Sources give slightly different historical names for the parade grounds that this space occupies.

This museum, which doubles as a Filipiniana research center, is known to hold works by artists such as Juan Luna, Fernando Amorsolo, Félix Hidalgo and Victorio Edades, along with stamps, coins, memorabilia and books. One blog (updated November 2024) lists hours of Tuesday–Saturday
and an admission of
for non-UP visitors. Details change often, so check before you go.

blocks.title: University chapel (Parish of the Holy Sacrifice)

children.text: A circular chapel designed by architect Leandro Locsin and completed in 1955, it is known for its concrete dome. Wikivoyage notes that it contains works by five National Artists and has been a National Historical Landmark since 2005. It stands on Apacible Street, and you should visit quietly during Mass.

The Lantern Parade, held in December just before the Christmas break, is the signature event: giant lanterns and floats made by colleges and student groups circle the Academic Oval, and the evening ends with performances and fireworks behind Quezon Hall. The UP Fair takes place at the Sunken Garden in February. Dates and venues change from year to year, so check the official UP Diliman announcements.

A self-guided walking tour created by UP's Asian Institute of Tourism, with audio commentary reached through QR codes. It takes you in order through Quezon Hall, Gonzalez Hall (the University Main Library) and the main buildings around the Oval, so you can understand the architecture and history without a guide. Bring your phone and earphones.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From the Oblation to the Sunken Garden

children.text: Enter from Commonwealth Avenue or Katipunan Avenue and see the Oblation statue in front of Quezon Hall. The morning light is good and it is not yet hot, which makes it ideal for photos.
Walk the Academic Oval, following the direction signs. One lap is about
2.2 km
, so even at a slow pace it takes around
40 minutes
. Look at the exteriors of Gonzalez Hall and Palma Hall as you pass.
Look around the Carillon tower, the UP Theater and the front of UP Cine Adarna. If you time it for the top of the hour, you can hear the bells.
Stroll through the Sunken Garden or rest in the shade, and if the Vargas Museum is open that day, step inside.
Have lunch at Rodic's Diner, an alumni-center café or the food park. Tapsilog and similar Filipino dishes are the staples.
Head off campus to Maginhawa Street to browse the cafés and restaurants, or shop at UP Town Center.
During the hottest hours (
), cut down on walking and slot in the indoor museum and restaurants.
Start at Quezon Hall and check the building names around the Oval one by one. Palma Hall and Melchor Hall, and Benitez Hall and Malcolm Hall, mirror each other.
See the exterior of Gonzalez Hall (the University Main Library). It was completed in 1950 and designed by Juan Nakpil.
Go to the university chapel on Apacible Street to see Locsin's circular design and concrete dome.
View modern Philippine painting at the Vargas Museum, where works by Juan Luna and Amorsolo are presented.
Many bus and jeepney routes run along Commonwealth Avenue from central Manila, Makati and Quezon City. Wikivoyage lists Philcoa (near Maginhawa Street) and UP Technohub as useful stops to get off.
The LRT-2 Katipunan station is at the corner of Katipunan Avenue and Aurora Boulevard, and from there you can walk, or take a tricycle or taxi, to the campus's eastern entrance.
On buses the conductor calls out the next stop, so tell them in advance where you want to get off. Travel times vary widely with traffic, so check locally.
Wikivoyage lists the MRT-7 UP station as a planned line. Check the latest announcements to see whether it has opened.
You can reach the campus by Grab or taxi from Manila airport (NAIA), Makati and BGC. During rush hours, travel time increases greatly.
If you set the destination to "Quezon Hall" or "Oblation," the driver will take you to the heart of the campus.
Ikot and Toki jeepneys run inside the UP campus and stop at main places such as the Oblation, Quezon Hall and the Sunken Garden. Check the latest information for the routes.
One lane of the Academic Oval is reserved for pedestrians and cyclists, which makes it good for walking or cycling around.

The dry season from November to May is best for walking. December to February is especially pleasant, with cool mornings and evenings on the Oval, the Lantern Parade in December and the UP Fair in February.

From March to May, daytime temperatures are very high, so walk early in the morning or around sunset. In the rainy season from June to November, showers are frequent in the afternoon, so bring an umbrella and include indoor museums and restaurants in your plan.

On campus, Rodic's Diner (open since 1949, at the Epsilon Chi Center next to Bahay ng Alumni) is famous for home-style dishes such as tapsilog, sinigang and dinuguan. It is listed as open daily

, but hours may change. The Art Circle Café and ROC at the alumni center serve pasta, coffee and Filipino dishes, and the Gyud Food food park across from the College of Fine Arts has many stalls gathered together.

Off campus, Maginhawa Street is the leading food-trip street, and Area 2 along J.P. Laurel Street is a budget-friendly strip for students. Banapple on Katipunan Avenue is known for its Banoffee pie. Gubat, which serves Filipino food on banana leaves, is also popular.

You will stay not on the campus but in a hotel or Airbnb in Quezon City. Many visitors base themselves in central Manila and make it a day trip. The Maginhawa side, the students' street, has many mid-range and budget lodgings.
The Academic Oval is coolest between
and
, and many residents jog then, so it feels lively.
To hear the Carillon, be near the tower on the hour or at the
and
performance times.
The Balik-Yapak self-guided tour uses QR codes for audio commentary, so you need mobile data and earphones.
The Vargas Museum is said to be closed on Mondays and Sundays. Check its open days before you go.
The campus is large, so bring comfortable shoes, a hat and water. Even with plenty of shade, it is hot during the day.
Restaurants on Maginhawa Street get crowded at lunch and dinner, so it is easier to go early or in the late afternoon.
During events (the Lantern Parade and the UP Fair), expect traffic restrictions and crowds, so use public transport and walk.
Check the official website announcements for UP Diliman's latest opening hours and visitor rules first.
UP Diliman is a real university where students study and live. During classes and exams, move quietly, and entry to buildings may be restricted.
Campus access, photography rules and event-period restrictions can change, so check the latest announcements from the UP Diliman website or the Diliman Information Office.
The university chapel is a place of worship where Mass is still held. Avoid revealing clothing and loud voices.
Taxi and Grab fares and waiting times can rise sharply during rush hours.
Museum fees and opening hours differ between sources, so check locally.
Jeepneys, pedestrians and cyclists share the same road on campus, so watch the direction of traffic on the Oval.
A leading park and monument in Quezon City, about
10–20 minutes
from Diliman by car. With walks, a museum and food, it pairs well with a campus visit.
Marikina is known as the center of the Philippine shoe industry. You can continue to it as a day trip after visiting the campus.
A mixed-use city district in eastern Quezon City where you can enjoy shopping, meals and the night view.
A food-trip street in UP Village right next to the campus, with a cluster of distinctive cafés and restaurants. It is within walking distance.
